# How to use this guide

Pharmacology I is a 7-unit course taught in Semester 3 of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing programme. It covers the principles of pharmacology and the main drug groups that nurses use most frequently. It is not examined on its own at the end of Semester 3 — only internal (sessional/college) marks are recorded now. The university examination comes next semester.

## This is a "Part I" course — no university exam this semester

**There is no end-semester university theory examination for Pharmacology I in Semester 3.** Only internal/sessional marks are recorded this semester, and they are **carried forward**. Pharmacology is examined by the university **together with Pharmacology II (Semester 4) and Pathology I + II and Genetics**, as one written paper in Semester 4.

That Semester 4 combined paper is **75 marks, 3 hours**:

| Section | Subject | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Pharmacology (Part I + Part II) | 38 |
| B | Pathology (Part I + Part II) | 25 |
| C | Genetics | 12 |

Confirm the exact breakdown with your college, as universities may vary the internal split.

The pharmacology you learn now (Part I) is re-tested together with the Part II content next semester. **Do not treat this semester's work as "over" once the sessional is done.** Revise it again when you study Pharmacology II.

The practice paper in this pack is modelled on the **Section A pharmacology** questions of the Semester 4 combined paper.

## How the unit files are arranged

The INC syllabus for Pharmacology I has eight numbered units. Because Units VII and VIII together are large, they have been split to keep each notes file manageable. The seven files map to the INC units as follows:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Main content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 | I | Introduction to pharmacology, pharmacodynamics (receptors, dose-response, efficacy, potency), pharmacokinetics (ADME), adverse drug reactions, drug interactions, pharmacovigilance |
| Unit 2 | II | Antiseptics and disinfectants; drugs acting on the GI system (antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers, antiemetics, laxatives, antidiarrhoeals) |
| Unit 3 | III | Drugs acting on the respiratory system (bronchodilators, antihistamines, corticosteroids, cough and cold preparations, oxygen); drugs acting on the skin (topical steroids, antifungals, antibacterials, retinoids) |
| Unit 4 | IV (a) | Autonomic nervous system drugs: cholinergic and anticholinergic; sympathomimetic and sympatholytic |
| Unit 5 | IV (b) | Cardiovascular drugs: antihypertensives, diuretics, anti-anginals, anti-arrhythmics, drugs for heart failure, anticoagulants |
| Unit 6 | V | Drugs for anaemia (iron, B12, folic acid, EPO), coagulation and bleeding, hypolipidaemic drugs, plasma expanders, drugs for shock |
| Unit 7 | VI / VII–VIII | Endocrine drugs (insulin, oral antidiabetics, thyroid, corticosteroids, sex hormones, oral contraceptives); drugs for infections (antibiotics, antitubercular, antifungal, antiviral, antiprotozoal, anthelmintic) |

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most years; often as a short answer (5 marks) or as part of a 10-mark essay. Know the classification, mechanism, uses, adverse effects and nursing points.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a broader question.
- **Low** — less common; tested in MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns in INC nursing pharmacology papers; they are not a promise.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Pharmacology basics | Routes of administration, first-pass effect, half-life, drug interactions (types), ADRs (types and examples), pharmacovigilance |
| 2 GI drugs | H2 blockers vs proton pump inhibitors (mechanism comparison), antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide), oral rehydration, laxatives (types and when to use) |
| 3 Respiratory and skin | Bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists vs methylxanthines), inhaler technique, antihistamines (sedating vs non-sedating), oxygen therapy types (nasal prongs, mask, Venturi) |
| 4 Autonomic | Atropine uses and side effects, adrenaline (epinephrine) in anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, beta-blockers (propranolol — contraindications in asthma), neostigmine |
| 5 Cardiovascular | ACE inhibitors (dry cough side effect), diuretics (frusemide — loop vs thiazide vs potassium-sparing), anticoagulants (heparin vs warfarin, reversal — protamine vs vitamin K), sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) for angina |
| 6 Blood and haematinics | Iron (oral iron with vitamin C, oral iron side effects, parenteral iron), classification of anaemia by aetiology, anticoagulant types and reversal |
| 7 Endocrine and anti-infectives | Insulin types (rapid, short, intermediate, long-acting), hypoglycaemia signs and management, penicillin allergy and anaphylaxis, antibiotics spectrum (penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, macrolides), TB drugs (HRZE), antimalarials, oral rehydration in cholera |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Classify drugs before describing them.** A classification table earns marks on its own and organises the rest of your answer.

2. **For every drug group, follow this structure**: Classification → Mechanism of action → Examples → Clinical uses → Adverse effects → Contraindications → Nursing responsibilities. Even a 5-mark answer improves when it follows this order.

3. **Know the high-alert drugs by heart**: insulin (types, hypoglycaemia), anticoagulants (bleeding risk, monitoring, reversal), antibiotics (allergy, culture before starting, complete the course), adrenaline (anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest doses and routes).

4. **Tables for comparisons score well**: H2 blockers vs PPIs, heparin vs warfarin, sedating vs non-sedating antihistamines, oral hypoglycaemic drug classes.

5. **Nursing responsibilities** must be included for every drug group. Examiners expect at least: check allergy, check relevant lab (BG for insulin, INR for warfarin), monitor for the drug's known adverse effect, teach the patient.

6. **For the MCQ section**, focus on: half-life, mechanism of action (which receptor or enzyme), one specific adverse effect per important drug, reversal agents (heparin → protamine, warfarin → vitamin K, opioids → naloxone, benzodiazepines → flumazenil).

7. **Exam reminder**: pharmacology is examined in Semester 4 as Section A (38 marks) of the combined 75-mark paper. The practice paper in this pack models that section.

# Last-night revision sheet

Pharmacology I is examined in Semester 4 as **Section A (38 marks)** of the combined 75-mark paper. Work through these summary tables and the MCQ bank tonight. You need classification, mechanism, one key adverse effect, and nursing responsibilities for each drug group.

---

**Pharmacokinetics — ADME key points**

| Step | Key term | Nurse's relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Absorption | First-pass effect: oral drugs metabolised in liver/gut wall before reaching circulation; reduces bioavailability; e.g. GTN, morphine → given sublingually or IV | Sublingual route bypasses first pass |
| Distribution | Volume of distribution (Vd): lipid-soluble drugs have large Vd (penetrate tissues); protein binding — only free drug is active | Warfarin is 99% protein-bound; drug interactions displace it → bleeding risk |
| Metabolism | CYP450 enzymes in liver; inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin) speed up metabolism; inhibitors (cimetidine, erythromycin) slow it | TB drugs (rifampicin) reduce effect of oral contraceptives |
| Excretion | Mostly renal; half-life (t½) = time for plasma level to fall by 50%; 5 half-lives to eliminate fully | Renal failure → drug accumulation; reduce dose (e.g. aminoglycosides, digoxin) |

---

**Autonomic drugs — quick reference**

| Drug type | Receptor | Main effects | Key examples | Nursing point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cholinergic (parasympathomimetic) | Muscarinic / nicotinic | ↓ HR, ↑ GI motility, miosis, bronchoconstriction, salivation | Pilocarpine (eye drops), neostigmine (reversal of neuromuscular block) | SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI cramps, Emesis (cholinergic excess) |
| Anticholinergic (parasympatholytic) | Muscarinic block | ↑ HR, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, dilated pupil | Atropine, hyoscine, glycopyrrolate | Atropine → tachycardia; contraindicated in glaucoma, BPH; antidote for organophosphate poisoning |
| Sympathomimetic (adrenergic) | α, β | α: vasoconstriction, ↑ BP; β1: ↑ HR, ↑ force; β2: bronchodilation | Adrenaline (α+β), noradrenaline (α), salbutamol (β2), dobutamine (β1) | Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM for anaphylaxis; also used in cardiac arrest (IV/IO) |
| Sympatholytic | α block / β block | β-blockers: ↓ HR, ↓ BP, bronchospasm | Propranolol (non-selective), atenolol (β1-selective), prazosin (α1-block) | β-blockers contraindicated in asthma; mask hypoglycaemia symptoms |

---

**Cardiovascular drug classes**

| Class | Mechanism | Examples | Key adverse effect | Nursing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ACE inhibitors | Block angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ angiotensin II → vasodilation, ↓ aldosterone | Ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril | Dry cough (bradykinin accumulation); hyperkalaemia; angioedema (rare — stop drug) | Monitor K+, renal function; avoid in pregnancy |
| ARBs | Block angiotensin II receptor | Losartan, valsartan | No dry cough; hyperkalaemia | Same monitoring as ACE inhibitors |
| Loop diuretics | Inhibit Na/K/2Cl in loop of Henle | Frusemide (furosemide) | Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, ototoxicity (high IV dose) | Monitor electrolytes; give in morning to avoid nocturnal diuresis |
| Thiazide diuretics | Inhibit NaCl in DCT | Hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide | Hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia | Give potassium supplement or combine with K-sparing diuretic |
| Potassium-sparing | Block aldosterone (spironolactone) or Na channels (amiloride) | Spironolactone, amiloride | Hyperkalaemia; spironolactone → gynaecomastia | Do not combine with ACE inhibitor without monitoring K+ |
| Calcium channel blockers | Block L-type calcium channels | Amlodipine, nifedipine (dihydropyridines — vasodilation); diltiazem, verapamil (also ↓ HR) | Ankle oedema (dihydropyridines); bradycardia (diltiazem/verapamil) | Verapamil contraindicated with beta-blockers (complete heart block risk) |
| GTN / organic nitrates | Release nitric oxide → venodilation, ↓ preload, coronary vasodilation | GTN sublingual, isosorbide dinitrate | Headache, flushing, postural hypotension; tolerance with long-acting forms | Sublingual GTN: sit/lie down, repeat up to 3 times at 5-min intervals; call ambulance if no relief after 1 tablet |
| Heparin | Activates antithrombin III → inhibits thrombin and Xa | UFH (IV/SC), LMWH (enoxaparin SC) | Bleeding; HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) | Monitor APTT (UFH); antidote = protamine sulphate; watch for bruising and blood in urine/stool |
| Warfarin | Inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) | Warfarin | Bleeding; teratogenic | Monitor INR (target 2–3 for most); antidote = vitamin K; many drug and food interactions (avoid cranberry juice, variable leafy veg intake) |
| Aspirin | Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 → ↓ thromboxane A2 | 75–100 mg for antiplatelet effect | GI bleeding; Reye's syndrome in children | Give with food; avoid in children <16 |

---

**Respiratory drugs**

| Drug | Class | Use | Adverse effect | Nursing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salbutamol (albuterol) | SABA (short-acting β2 agonist) | Acute bronchospasm | Tremor, tachycardia | Demonstrate inhaler technique; spacer in children and elderly |
| Ipratropium | SAMA (short-acting muscarinic antagonist) | COPD, combined with SABA | Dry mouth, blurred vision | Avoid eye contact with spray |
| Theophylline | Methylxanthine | COPD, asthma (oral) | Narrow therapeutic index; arrhythmia, seizures at toxic levels | Monitor plasma level (10–20 mg/L); many interactions |
| Beclomethasone, budesonide | Inhaled corticosteroid | Maintenance of asthma | Oral candidiasis, dysphonia | Rinse mouth after each use |
| Chlorpheniramine (sedating H1 blocker) | First-generation antihistamine | Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus | Sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention | Warn about driving |
| Cetirizine, loratadine | Second-generation antihistamine | As above | Minimal sedation | Preferred for daytime |
| Dextromethorphan | Cough suppressant | Dry cough | Drowsiness | Do not use for productive cough |

---

**Anti-infectives — summary table**

| Class | Mechanism | Key examples | Spectrum | Major adverse effect | Nurse's point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Penicillins | Cell-wall synthesis inhibition | Amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, benzylpenicillin | Gram+ mostly; amoxicillin broader | **Allergy/anaphylaxis** | Ask allergy history; keep adrenaline ready after injection |
| Cephalosporins | Cell-wall (beta-lactam) | Cefalexin (1st gen), ceftriaxone (3rd gen) | Broad; later gens more Gram- | Allergy (cross-react with penicillin ~10%) | Monitor renal function |
| Aminoglycosides | Protein synthesis (30S) | Gentamicin, amikacin, streptomycin | Gram- (aerobic) | **Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity** | Monitor renal function and hearing; keep well-hydrated |
| Macrolides | Protein synthesis (50S) | Erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin | Gram+ + atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) | GI upset; CYP inhibition | Give with food |
| Fluoroquinolones | DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV | Ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin | Broad Gram- and some Gram+ | Tendon rupture (Achilles), QT prolongation | Avoid in growing children, pregnancy; take 2 h after antacids |
| Tetracyclines | Protein synthesis (30S) | Doxycycline | Broad; Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, rickettsiae, malaria prophylaxis | Dental staining / bone in children; photosensitivity | Avoid in children <8, pregnancy; take with full glass of water, upright |
| Metronidazole | DNA strand breakage | Metronidazole | Anaerobes, protozoa (Giardia, amoebiasis, trichomonas) | Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste | No alcohol during and 48 h after course |
| Sulfonamides + trimethoprim | Folate synthesis | Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) | Broad; PCP treatment and prophylaxis | Allergy, marrow suppression, hyperkalaemia | Adequate hydration; avoid in G6PD deficiency |

**TB drugs (HRZE)**: Isoniazid (H) — give pyridoxine; Rifampicin (R) — orange urine is normal, monitor LFT; Pyrazinamide (Z) — monitor LFT and uric acid; Ethambutol (E) — monthly vision check.

**Antimalarials**: chloroquine (P. vivax); ACT (artesunate combinations) for P. falciparum; primaquine for radical cure of vivax (check G6PD first); lumefantrine (with artemether) — take with fatty food.

---

**Insulin types**

| Type | Onset | Peak | Duration | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rapid-acting (aspart, lispro) | 15 min | 1–2 h | 3–5 h | Mealtime; can give just after food |
| Short-acting (regular/soluble) | 30–60 min | 2–4 h | 6–8 h | Pre-meal 30 min; IV infusion for DKA |
| Intermediate (NPH, isophane) | 1–2 h | 4–8 h | 12–18 h | Twice daily basal |
| Long-acting (glargine, detemir) | 1–2 h | Flat / no peak | 20–24 h | Once daily basal; do NOT mix in same syringe |

Hypoglycaemia (BG <70 mg/dL): give 15 g fast glucose (glucose tablets, juice, sugar water) → recheck in 15 min → repeat if still low; if unconscious → IV dextrose 25% or glucagon IM.

---

**Nurse's responsibilities with any drug (5 Rs + 2)**

Right Patient → Right Drug → Right Dose → Right Route → Right Time + Right Documentation + Check Allergy.

Before giving: check allergy, check relevant lab (BG for insulin, INR for warfarin, APTT for heparin, ECG for QT-prolonging drugs), explain the drug and its side effects to the patient.
After giving: document, observe for desired effect and adverse effects.

---

**Exam reminder**: Pharmacology I is examined in Semester 4 combined paper, Section A, 38 marks. High-priority: insulin types, ACE inhibitor cough, anticoagulant reversal (protamine for heparin; vitamin K for warfarin), penicillin anaphylaxis (adrenaline), adrenaline in cardiac arrest. Classify first, then mechanism, uses, ADR, nursing.

# Unit 1: Introduction to pharmacology, pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics

INC Unit I (3 hours): definitions and branches, nature and sources of drugs, dosage forms and routes, terminology, classification, abbreviations, prescription, drug calculation, weights and measures, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, principles of drug administration, the Indian Pharmacopoeia and drug laws, rational use of drugs and principles of therapeutics. This unit is the base for every drug you meet later, so learn its terms well.

## 1.1 Definitions and branches

- **Drug** (WHO): any substance or product that is used or intended to be used to modify or explore physiological systems or pathological states for the benefit of the recipient. Drugs are used to prevent, diagnose or treat disease.
- **Pharmacology**: the science of drugs and their interaction with living systems — what a drug does to the body and what the body does to the drug.
- **Medicine**: a drug in a form ready to give to a patient (tablet, injection, syrup).

| Branch | What it studies |
| --- | --- |
| Pharmacodynamics | What the drug does to the body: actions and mechanism of action |
| Pharmacokinetics | What the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME) |
| Pharmacotherapeutics | Use of drugs to prevent and treat disease |
| Chemotherapy | Drugs that kill or stop the growth of microbes, parasites and cancer cells |
| Toxicology | Harmful effects of chemicals and drugs, their detection and treatment |
| Clinical pharmacology | Study of drugs in human beings, healthy and sick |
| Pharmacy | Preparing, compounding and dispensing medicines |
| Pharmacognosy | Drugs obtained from natural sources, mainly plants |
| Pharmacogenetics | How inherited differences change drug response |
| Pharmacoepidemiology | Use and effects of drugs in large populations |

## 1.2 Nature and sources of drugs

Drugs may be solids, liquids or gases; most are weak acids or weak bases, which affects how they are absorbed and excreted.

| Source | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Plants | Morphine (opium poppy), atropine (belladonna), digoxin (foxglove), quinine (cinchona bark) |
| Animals | Heparin, older insulins (pork and beef pancreas), thyroid extract |
| Minerals | Iron salts, magnesium sulfate, liquid paraffin, kaolin |
| Microorganisms | Penicillin (Penicillium mould), streptomycin (Streptomyces) |
| Synthetic | Paracetamol, sulfonamides, most modern drugs |
| Semi-synthetic | Ampicillin, amoxicillin (built on a natural nucleus) |
| Biotechnology (recombinant DNA) | Human insulin, hepatitis B vaccine, erythropoietin |

## 1.3 Dosage forms

| Group | Dosage forms |
| --- | --- |
| Solid | Tablets (plain, film- or enteric-coated, sustained-release, dispersible, sublingual), capsules, powders, granules, lozenges |
| Liquid (oral) | Syrups, elixirs, suspensions (shake well), emulsions, solutions, drops |
| Semi-solid (topical) | Ointments, creams, gels, pastes, lotions |
| Parenteral | Injections (ampoules, vials, prefilled syringes), infusions |
| Others | Suppositories (rectal), pessaries (vaginal), inhalers and nebuliser solutions, transdermal patches, eye and ear drops, implants |

Nursing points: never crush enteric-coated or sustained-release tablets (the coating protects the stomach or controls release); shake suspensions; store as the label says (insulin and vaccines in the refrigerator, not frozen).

## 1.4 Routes of drug administration

```text
                ROUTES
   ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
 Local         Systemic: enteral   Systemic: parenteral
 (topical,     (oral, sublingual,  (IV, IM, SC, intradermal,
 eye, ear,     buccal, rectal)     intrathecal, intra-articular,
 inhaled for                       inhalation for general
 lungs)                            effect, transdermal)
```

| Route | Advantages | Disadvantages / nursing points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral | Safe, cheap, painless, self-administered | Slow; first-pass metabolism; not for vomiting or unconscious patients; irritant drugs cause nausea |
| Sublingual / buccal | Quick; avoids first-pass metabolism | Only small, lipid-soluble drugs (glyceryl trinitrate); patient must not swallow |
| Rectal | Useful in vomiting or unconscious patients, children | Irregular absorption; may irritate |
| Intravenous (IV) | Fastest, 100% bioavailability, exact control, large volumes | Cannot be recalled; risk of infection, thrombophlebitis, air embolism, extravasation, speed shock |
| Intramuscular (IM) | Depot and oily preparations; faster than SC | Painful; nerve injury if wrong site; avoid in bleeding disorders |
| Subcutaneous (SC) | Self-injection (insulin, heparin) | Small volumes; slow in shock |
| Intradermal | Skin tests, BCG vaccine | Very small volume |
| Inhalation | Direct action on airways, fewer systemic effects | Needs correct technique |
| Transdermal | Steady levels over a long time | Skin irritation; rotate sites |
| Topical | Local action | Some may be absorbed through broken skin |

## 1.5 Terms used in pharmacology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Dose | The amount of drug given at one time |
| Therapeutic effect | The intended beneficial effect |
| Side effect | Unwanted but expected effect at a normal dose (dry mouth with atropine) |
| Adverse effect | Any harmful, unintended effect |
| Toxic effect | Harmful effect from excess drug or accumulation |
| Idiosyncrasy | Unusual, genetically based reaction (haemolysis with primaquine in G6PD deficiency) |
| Allergy (hypersensitivity) | Immune reaction to a drug, not related to dose (penicillin anaphylaxis) |
| Tolerance | Larger amount needed for the same effect after repeated use (nitrates, opioids) |
| Tachyphylaxis | Rapid tolerance after a few closely spaced doses (ephedrine) |
| Cumulation | Build-up of a slowly eliminated drug (digoxin) |
| Dependence | Need to keep taking the drug; withdrawal symptoms on stopping |
| Teratogenicity | Ability to cause birth defects (thalidomide, warfarin) |
| Iatrogenic disease | Disease caused by treatment |
| Placebo | Inert substance that can still produce a response through expectation |
| Half-life (t½) | Time taken for the plasma concentration to fall by half |
| Therapeutic index | Ratio of the toxic to the effective dose; a narrow index means a small margin of safety (digoxin, lithium, warfarin) |

## 1.6 Classification of drugs

Drugs can be grouped in several ways; each is useful for a different purpose.

- **By the system acted on**: drugs acting on the CNS, cardiovascular system, GI tract.
- **By therapeutic use**: antihypertensives, analgesics, antimicrobials.
- **By mechanism**: β-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, ACE inhibitors.
- **By chemical structure**: penicillins, sulfonamides, benzodiazepines.
- **By legal status**: prescription (Schedule H, H1, X) and non-prescription (over-the-counter) drugs.

A drug has three names: chemical name (exact structure), **generic (non-proprietary) name** (paracetamol) and **brand (trade) name** given by a company. Nurses should know generic names; one generic drug can be sold under many brands, which is a common cause of double dosing.

## 1.7 Abbreviations used in prescriptions

| Abbreviation | Meaning | Abbreviation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rx | Take (recipe) | stat | Immediately, once |
| OD | Once a day | SOS | If needed, once |
| BD / BID | Twice a day | PRN | When required |
| TDS / TID | Three times a day | ac | Before food |
| QID | Four times a day | pc | After food |
| HS | At bedtime | PO | By mouth |
| IM / IV / SC | Intramuscular / intravenous / subcutaneous | SL | Sublingual |
| NPO / NBM | Nothing by mouth | gtt | Drops |

Safety: write "units" in full (a handwritten "U" can be read as 0), avoid trailing zeros ("1.0" may be read as 10) and always put a zero before a decimal point (0.5). Unclear orders must be clarified with the prescriber before giving.

## 1.8 Prescription

A prescription is a written order from a registered medical practitioner for a medicine for a named patient.

```text
 Name, qualification, registration number, address of prescriber
 Date
 Patient: name, age, sex, weight, address
 Superscription:  Rx
 Inscription:     drug name, strength, dosage form
 Subscription:    instructions to the pharmacist (how much to dispense)
 Signa (transcription): instructions to the patient — dose, route, frequency, duration
 Signature of the prescriber
```

In hospital the nurse works from the doctor's medication order sheet. A **standing order** is to be carried out until cancelled; a **stat order** once immediately; a **PRN order** when needed within limits; a **verbal or telephone order** only in emergencies, read back and signed by the doctor as soon as possible.

## 1.9 Weights, measures and drug calculation

**Metric system** (used in India):

| Unit | Equals |
| --- | --- |
| 1 kilogram (kg) | 1000 grams (g) |
| 1 gram (g) | 1000 milligrams (mg) |
| 1 milligram (mg) | 1000 micrograms (µg or mcg) |
| 1 litre (L) | 1000 millilitres (mL) |
| 1 mL | about 1 cubic centimetre (cc) |

Some drugs are measured in **units** (insulin, heparin) or **international units** (vitamin D). Household spoons are not accurate; use a marked measuring cup or oral syringe.

**Basic formula for tablets and liquids**

```text
 Amount to give = (Dose ordered ÷ Strength available) × Quantity (volume) it comes in
                 = (D ÷ H) × Q
```

Practice example with an imaginary "Drug X" (figures for arithmetic practice only): ordered 250 mg; stock 500 mg in 5 mL → (250 ÷ 500) × 5 = 2.5 mL.

**IV infusion rate**

```text
 Drops per minute = Total volume (mL) × Drop factor (drops/mL) ÷ Time (minutes)
 mL per hour      = Total volume (mL) ÷ Time (hours)
```

Drop factor: standard (macro) sets about 15 or 20 drops/mL (check the pack); microdrip (paediatric) sets 60 drops/mL. Example: 1000 mL over 8 hours with a 20 drops/mL set → 1000 × 20 ÷ 480 ≈ 42 drops per minute.

**Children's dose formulas** (rarely used now; dosing is by kg or body surface area from a reference):

- Young's rule: child dose = (age in years ÷ (age + 12)) × adult dose.
- Clark's rule: child dose = (weight in kg ÷ 70) × adult dose.
- Body surface area: child dose = (BSA in m² ÷ 1.73) × adult dose.

Always have a second nurse check calculations for high-alert drugs (insulin, heparin, potassium chloride infusion, chemotherapy, paediatric doses).

## 1.10 Pharmacodynamics

Pharmacodynamics is the study of drug actions and how they are produced.

**Types of action**: stimulation (adrenaline on the heart), depression (diazepam on the brain), irritation (counter-irritants), replacement (insulin in diabetes, iron in anaemia), and killing of microbes or cancer cells (cytotoxic action).

**Mechanisms of action**

1. **On receptors** — most drugs. A receptor is a protein on or in a cell to which a drug binds to start a response.
   - Agonist: binds and activates (salbutamol on β2 receptors).
   - Antagonist: binds but does not activate; blocks the agonist (atropine blocks muscarinic receptors).
   - Partial agonist: produces less than the maximum response (buprenorphine).
2. **On enzymes** — inhibit an enzyme (aspirin on cyclo-oxygenase, neostigmine on cholinesterase, ACE inhibitors).
3. **On ion channels** — calcium channel blockers (amlodipine), local anaesthetics block sodium channels.
4. **On transporters/pumps** — omeprazole blocks the proton pump, digoxin blocks Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, furosemide blocks a co-transporter in the kidney.
5. **Physical or chemical action** — antacids neutralise acid; osmotic laxatives hold water; activated charcoal adsorbs.

**Combined effects of drugs**

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Additive | Effect equals the sum (1 + 1 = 2) | Two antacids |
| Synergism | Effect greater than the sum (1 + 1 > 2) | Sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim; alcohol + sedatives |
| Potentiation | One drug with no effect of its own increases another's | Carbidopa increases levodopa effect |
| Antagonism | One drug reduces another's effect | Atropine vs acetylcholine; naloxone vs morphine; protamine vs heparin (chemical) |

Types of antagonism: physical (charcoal adsorbs), chemical (antacid neutralises acid; protamine binds heparin), physiological (adrenaline reverses histamine's bronchospasm through different receptors), receptor (atropine vs acetylcholine — competitive).

**Tolerance** may be natural or acquired; **cross-tolerance** occurs between related drugs (alcohol and sedatives).

**Therapeutic, adverse and toxic effects.** Every drug has a range between the dose that helps and the dose that harms. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (digoxin, warfarin, lithium, aminoglycosides, theophylline) need close monitoring of signs and sometimes blood levels.

**Pharmacovigilance** (WHO): the science and activities relating to detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects or any other drug-related problem. In India the **Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI)** is coordinated by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad, with ADR monitoring centres in hospitals. Nurses can and should report suspected adverse drug reactions on the ADR reporting form.

## 1.11 Pharmacokinetics

```text
 Drug given → ABSORPTION → blood → DISTRIBUTION → tissues / site of action
                                ↓
                      METABOLISM (mainly liver)
                                ↓
                      EXCRETION (mainly kidney; also bile, lungs, milk, sweat)
```

**Absorption** — movement of a drug from the site of administration into the blood. Faster with lipid-soluble, un-ionised, small molecules, a large absorbing area and good blood flow. Food can slow or reduce absorption (give tetracyclines away from milk and antacids). Shock reduces absorption from IM and SC sites.

**Bioavailability** — the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. IV = 100%. Oral may be less because of incomplete absorption and **first-pass metabolism** (drug absorbed from the gut passes through the liver first and part is destroyed — glyceryl trinitrate is therefore given sublingually).

**Distribution** — spread from blood to tissues. Factors: plasma protein binding (bound drug is inactive and stays in the blood; displacement by another drug can cause toxicity, e.g. warfarin displaced by aspirin), lipid solubility, blood flow, and barriers:
- Blood–brain barrier: only lipid-soluble drugs enter easily.
- Placental barrier: most drugs cross — care in pregnancy.
- Drugs also pass into breast milk.

**Metabolism (biotransformation)** — chemical change of a drug, mainly in the liver, usually making it more water-soluble and easier to excrete.
- Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis (often by cytochrome P450 enzymes).
- Phase II: conjugation (glucuronide, sulfate, acetyl) — products are usually inactive.
- A **prodrug** is inactive until metabolised (enalapril → enalaprilat; levodopa → dopamine).
- **Enzyme inducers** (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, alcohol, smoking) speed metabolism of other drugs → reduced effect (oral contraceptive failure with rifampicin).
- **Enzyme inhibitors** (cimetidine, erythromycin, ketoconazole, ciprofloxacin) slow metabolism → toxicity of the other drug.
- Newborns and elderly people and those with liver disease metabolise drugs slowly.

**Excretion** — removal from the body. Kidney (most drugs: glomerular filtration and tubular secretion; reabsorption depends on urine pH), bile and faeces, lungs (anaesthetic gases), breast milk, saliva and sweat. In kidney disease many drugs accumulate and doses are reduced by the doctor.

**Drug interactions** — change in the effect of one drug by another drug, food or alcohol.
- Pharmacokinetic: absorption (antacids or iron bind tetracycline), distribution (protein-binding displacement), metabolism (induction or inhibition), excretion (probenecid prolongs penicillin).
- Pharmacodynamic: additive or opposing effects (sedatives with alcohol; β-blockers block salbutamol).
- Pharmaceutical: incompatibility outside the body — do not mix drugs in one syringe or infusion unless known to be compatible.

**Key kinetic terms**: plasma half-life decides dosing frequency; about 4–5 half-lives are needed to reach a steady state with regular dosing (and to clear a drug after stopping); a **loading dose** is used when an effect is needed quickly; a **maintenance dose** keeps the level steady.

## 1.12 Principles of drug administration and individualising treatment

**Rights of medication administration** — the classic five rights are right patient, right drug, right dose, right route and right time; many hospitals add right documentation, right reason, right response, right to refuse and right education.

Nursing principles:
1. Check the order; clarify anything unclear.
2. Check the drug label three times (when taking it from storage, when preparing, before returning or discarding the container).
3. Identify the patient with two identifiers (name and hospital number), not the bed number.
4. Ask about allergies before the first dose.
5. Prepare and give medicines yourself; never give a drug prepared by someone else.
6. Check expiry date, colour and clarity.
7. Stay until oral medicines are swallowed.
8. Record immediately after giving — never before.
9. Observe for therapeutic and adverse effects and report.
10. Report and record any medication error at once.

**Factors that affect dose and response** (why treatment must be individualised):

| Factor | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Age | Newborns and the elderly have less liver and kidney capacity; the elderly take many drugs |
| Body weight / surface area | Children's doses are calculated by weight |
| Sex and pregnancy | Some drugs harm the fetus; drugs in labour affect the newborn |
| Route | Magnesium sulfate is a laxative by mouth but acts on the nervous system when injected |
| Disease | Liver disease slows metabolism; kidney disease slows excretion |
| Genetics | Slow acetylators get isoniazid neuropathy; G6PD deficiency |
| Tolerance and dependence | More drug needed for the same effect |
| Psychological factors | Placebo response; trust in the nurse |
| Other drugs and food | Interactions |
| Time of administration | Hypnotics at bedtime; some drugs before or after food |

## 1.13 Indian Pharmacopoeia, drug laws and schedule drugs

**Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP)** — the official book of standards for drugs in India: identity, purity and strength of drugs and how to test them. It is published by the **Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), Ghaziabad**, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and it is legally recognised under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. New editions appear every few years (IP 2022 is a recent edition; check the current one).

**Main Indian drug laws**

| Law | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 | Control of import, manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs and cosmetics; standards of quality; schedules |
| Pharmacy Act, 1948 | Regulates the profession of pharmacy; registration of pharmacists |
| Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 | Control of narcotic and psychotropic drugs (morphine, pethidine); strict storage and records |
| Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 | Stops misleading advertisements for cures |
| New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 | Approval of new drugs and conduct of clinical trials |

**Schedules under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules** (most asked in nursing exams):

| Schedule | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| G | Drugs to be taken only under medical supervision; label carries a caution |
| H | Prescription-only drugs; label carries "Rx" and the warning that they are to be sold on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner only |
| H1 | Selected antibiotics, anti-TB and habit-forming drugs; sold only on prescription with a boxed warning in red, and the pharmacist keeps a separate record of each sale |
| X | Narcotic and psychotropic drugs with the strictest control; labelled "XRx"; the pharmacist keeps a copy of the prescription |
| K | Drugs and situations exempted from certain provisions of the Act (for example some household remedies, and drugs supplied in certain government health programmes) — check the exact items in the current Rules |
| C and C1 | Biological products (vaccines, sera, insulin) needing special storage |
| M | Good manufacturing practices |

Nursing responsibilities: keep narcotic and controlled drugs in a **double-locked cupboard**, count and record them at every shift handover, sign the register for each dose with a witness, and return unused or wasted drug as per hospital policy.

## 1.14 Rational use of drugs and principles of therapeutics

**Rational use of medicines** (WHO): patients receive medicines appropriate to their clinical needs, in doses that meet their own individual requirements, for an adequate period of time, and at the lowest cost to them and their community.

Irrational practices: too many drugs (polypharmacy), unnecessary antibiotics and injections, self-medication, wrong dose or duration, fixed-dose combinations without reason, not following treatment.

**Essential medicines** are those that satisfy the priority health care needs of the population. India's **National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)** guides hospital supply and pricing; the latest revision is NLEM 2022.

**Principles of therapeutics**

1. Make a correct diagnosis and know the goal of treatment.
2. Choose the drug by effectiveness, safety, suitability for the patient and cost.
3. Prefer one drug where possible; use generic names.
4. Choose the right dose, route, frequency and duration for the patient.
5. Explain the treatment and warn about common side effects.
6. Monitor the response and adverse effects, and stop drugs no longer needed.

**Role of the nurse in drug therapy**: safe storage and administration, observation of effects and adverse reactions, patient teaching (purpose, how and when to take, what to avoid, side effects to report, completing the course), maintaining records, reporting errors and ADRs, and supporting adherence.

## Remember

- Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body; pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME).
- IV route gives 100% bioavailability; sublingual avoids first-pass metabolism.
- Agonist activates, antagonist blocks, partial agonist gives a submaximal response.
- Enzyme inducers (rifampicin) reduce other drugs' effects; enzyme inhibitors (cimetidine, erythromycin) increase them.
- Narrow therapeutic index: digoxin, warfarin, lithium, theophylline, aminoglycosides.
- D ÷ H × Q for dose; volume × drop factor ÷ minutes for drops per minute.
- Schedule H = prescription only; H1 = stricter with a sales record; X = strictest (narcotics and psychotropics); G = medical supervision; K = exemptions.
- IP is published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad; PvPI collects ADR reports.
- Rights of administration: patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation (and more).

# Unit 2: Antiseptics, disinfectants and drugs acting on the GI system

INC Unit II (1 hour) — commonly used antiseptics and disinfectants — joined here with INC Unit III (2 hours) — emetics and antiemetics, laxatives and purgatives, antacids and antipeptic ulcer drugs, antidiarrhoeals with fluid and electrolyte therapy, furazolidone and dicyclomine. For every drug group learn the action, uses, contraindications, interactions, side effects and the nurse's role. Doses are not given here; follow the prescriber's order and your hospital's formulary.

## 2.1 Terms used in infection control

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Sterilisation | Killing or removal of all microorganisms, including spores |
| Disinfection | Killing of most pathogenic organisms (not necessarily spores) on non-living objects |
| Disinfectant | Chemical used on inanimate objects and surfaces (floors, instruments) |
| Antiseptic | Chemical safe enough to use on living tissue (skin, wounds, mucous membranes) |
| Germicide (-cidal) | Kills microbes: bactericidal, fungicidal, virucidal, sporicidal |
| Bacteriostatic | Stops multiplication without killing |
| Sanitiser | Lowers microbial numbers to a safe level (hand rub, dishwashing) |
| Asepsis | Absence of infection; techniques that prevent contamination |

The same chemical may be a disinfectant at a strong concentration and an antiseptic when diluted.

**An ideal antiseptic/disinfectant** has a wide spectrum, acts quickly, works in the presence of blood and pus, is not irritant or toxic to tissues, does not corrode instruments or stain, is stable, cheap and pleasant to use.

**Factors affecting action**: concentration, contact time, temperature, number and type of organisms (spores and mycobacteria resist most chemicals), presence of organic matter (blood and pus reduce action, so clean first), pH and compatibility (soap inactivates chlorhexidine and cetrimide).

**Spaulding classification** for equipment: critical items entering sterile tissue (surgical instruments) → sterilise; semi-critical items touching mucous membranes (endoscopes) → high-level disinfection (for example glutaraldehyde); non-critical items touching intact skin (BP cuffs, bed rails) → low-level disinfection.

## 2.2 Commonly used antiseptics and disinfectants

| Group | Examples | Action | Uses | Points to note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alcohols | Ethyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol (70% is most effective) | Denature proteins | Skin before injection, hand rub, thermometers | Not sporicidal; flammable; dries skin; let it dry before injecting |
| Halogens – iodine | Tincture iodine, povidone-iodine | Oxidation of proteins | Pre-operative skin, wounds, surgical scrub | Stains; allergy; avoid large areas in newborns and in thyroid disease |
| Halogens – chlorine | Sodium hypochlorite (bleach), bleaching powder | Oxidation | Blood spills, surfaces, water disinfection, linen | Corrodes metal; inactivated by organic matter; never mix with acids (toxic chlorine gas) |
| Biguanides | Chlorhexidine (with cetrimide in Savlon) | Damages cell membrane | Hand wash, surgical scrub, mouthwash, catheter care | Inactivated by soap; may stain teeth; avoid eyes and ears |
| Quaternary ammonium | Cetrimide, benzalkonium chloride | Detergent, damages membrane | Wound cleaning, preservative | Inactivated by soap; weak against Gram-negatives |
| Phenols | Phenol, cresol (Lysol), chloroxylenol (Dettol) | Protein denaturation | Floors, excreta, linen (cresol); skin (chloroxylenol) | Phenol is corrosive to skin; standard for testing others (phenol coefficient) |
| Aldehydes | Glutaraldehyde (2%), formaldehyde (formalin) | Alkylate proteins | Endoscopes, heat-sensitive items; fumigation of rooms | Irritant to eyes and lungs; use in ventilated area with PPE; rinse items with sterile water |
| Oxidising agents | Hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate | Release oxygen | Wound cleaning (H₂O₂ froths and loosens debris); KMnO₄ soaks for weeping skin | Store away from light; KMnO₄ stains; use only freshly made, fully dissolved pale solutions |
| Dyes | Gentian violet, acriflavine | Act on cell wall | Fungal skin and mouth lesions, superficial wounds | Stains |
| Heavy metals | Silver nitrate, silver sulfadiazine | Bind proteins | Burns (silver sulfadiazine, Unit 3) | Silver nitrate stains black |
| Gas | Ethylene oxide | Alkylation | Sterilising heat-sensitive plastics | Toxic, explosive; items need aeration |
| Acids | Boric acid | Weak bacteriostatic | Old eye and ear washes | Rarely used now |

**Phenol coefficient (Rideal–Walker test)**: compares the killing power of a disinfectant with phenol under set conditions; a coefficient above 1 means it is stronger than phenol.

**Nursing responsibilities with antiseptics and disinfectants**

1. Use the agent and dilution set by the hospital infection control policy; label every container with name, strength, date and time of preparation.
2. Make dilutions freshly; discard old solutions (diluted solutions can grow bacteria such as Pseudomonas).
3. Clean before disinfecting — organic matter inactivates most agents.
4. Allow the full contact time; let skin antiseptics dry before a procedure.
5. Wear gloves, apron and eye protection with irritant chemicals (glutaraldehyde, phenol, bleach); keep the area ventilated.
6. Ask about allergy (iodine); watch for skin irritation and report.
7. Never use disinfectants on skin or wounds; never mix chemicals (bleach with acid or ammonia).
8. Store tightly closed, away from light and heat; keep out of reach of children and confused patients.

## 2.3 Emetics

Emetics produce vomiting. They act on the stomach (local irritants) or the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Inducing vomiting is now rarely recommended, because it delays better treatment and can cause aspiration. It must never be done in an unconscious or drowsy patient or after swallowing corrosives or kerosene. Ipecacuanha syrup and apomorphine are the classic examples you may be asked to name.

## 2.4 Antiemetics

Vomiting is coordinated by the **vomiting centre** in the medulla, which receives input from the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ), the gut (via 5-HT₃ receptors on vagal nerves), the inner ear (motion sickness) and the higher centres (smell, fear).

```text
 Gut irritation (chemotherapy, infection) → 5-HT₃ → vagus ─┐
 Drugs, toxins in blood → CTZ (D₂, 5-HT₃, NK₁) ──────────┼→ VOMITING CENTRE → vomiting
 Motion → inner ear (H₁, muscarinic) ────────────────────┤
 Anxiety, smell, pain → cortex ──────────────────────────┘
```

| Class | Examples | Main uses | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5-HT₃ antagonists | Ondansetron, granisetron | Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and post-operative vomiting | Headache, constipation, QT prolongation |
| D₂ antagonists (prokinetic) | Metoclopramide, domperidone | Gastritis, post-operative vomiting, migraine, gastroparesis | Metoclopramide: restlessness, acute dystonia (more in children and young adults); domperidone hardly enters the brain |
| Phenothiazines | Prochlorperazine, promethazine | Vertigo, drug-induced vomiting | Sedation, low BP, extrapyramidal effects |
| H₁ antihistamines | Promethazine, dimenhydrinate, meclizine, cyclizine | Motion sickness, vomiting of pregnancy (doxylamine with pyridoxine) | Drowsiness, dry mouth |
| Anticholinergic | Hyoscine (scopolamine), including a skin patch | Motion sickness | Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention |
| NK₁ antagonist | Aprepitant | Chemotherapy (with ondansetron and dexamethasone) | Fatigue |
| Corticosteroid | Dexamethasone | Chemotherapy-induced vomiting (add-on) | See Unit 6 |

**Nursing responsibilities**: assess the cause, amount and character of vomit and record intake and output; give the antiemetic before the trigger (before chemotherapy, about half an hour before travel); keep the patient in a lateral position if drowsy to prevent aspiration; mouth care; monitor for dehydration and electrolyte loss; watch for abnormal movements after metoclopramide and report; warn about drowsiness (no driving).

## 2.5 Laxatives and purgatives

A **laxative** produces soft formed stool gently; a **purgative (cathartic)** produces more fluid, frequent evacuation. Many drugs are laxatives in small amounts and purgatives in larger amounts.

| Class | Examples | How they work | Points to note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bulk-forming | Ispaghula (psyllium) husk, methylcellulose, bran | Absorb water, increase stool bulk, stimulate peristalsis | Take with plenty of water, or they may obstruct; act in 1–3 days |
| Stool softeners / lubricants | Docusate, liquid paraffin | Soften and lubricate stool | Liquid paraffin: risk of lipid pneumonia if aspirated (not at bedtime lying down, not in children and the elderly); reduces vitamin A, D, E, K absorption |
| Osmotic | Lactulose, magnesium salts, polyethylene glycol, sodium phosphate (enema) | Hold water in the gut by osmosis | Lactulose also used in hepatic encephalopathy (reduces ammonia absorption); bloating; electrolyte disturbance; magnesium salts avoided in kidney failure |
| Stimulant | Bisacodyl, senna, castor oil | Irritate the bowel and increase motility | Cramps; long use can damage the colon |
| Others | Glycerin suppository, enemas | Local action in the rectum | Quick action |

**Uses**: constipation (after diet and fluid advice fail), bowel preparation before surgery or colonoscopy, after anal surgery or myocardial infarction to avoid straining, hepatic encephalopathy (lactulose), drug-induced constipation (opioids).

**Contraindications**: undiagnosed abdominal pain, suspected appendicitis, intestinal obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease in a flare.

**Laxative abuse**: dehydration, low potassium, weakness, dependence and an atonic ("lazy") colon.

**Nursing**: assess bowel habits, diet and fluids first; teach fibre, fluids, exercise and a regular toilet time; give bulk laxatives with a full glass of water; give stimulant laxatives at bedtime for a morning effect; record bowel movements; watch for diarrhoea, cramps and electrolyte loss.

## 2.6 Antacids and anti-peptic ulcer drugs

Peptic ulcer results from an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, *Helicobacter pylori*, NSAIDs, smoking) and protective factors (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow).

```text
 Parietal cell acid secretion is stimulated by:
   Histamine (H₂) ─┐
   Acetylcholine (M₃) ─┼→ PROTON PUMP (H⁺/K⁺-ATPase) → HCl
   Gastrin ─────────┘
 H₂ blockers act on one input; PPIs block the final common step.
```

| Group | Examples | Action | Important points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Antacids – systemic | Sodium bicarbonate | Neutralise acid quickly | Absorbed → alkalosis; CO₂ causes belching; sodium load (avoid in heart failure, hypertension) |
| Antacids – non-systemic | Magnesium hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide, calcium carbonate | Neutralise acid | Mg causes diarrhoea, Al causes constipation, so they are combined; Al binds phosphate; calcium can cause rebound acid |
| H₂-receptor blockers | Famotidine, cimetidine | Block histamine on parietal cells | Cimetidine inhibits liver enzymes (interactions) and may cause gynaecomastia |
| Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) | Omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole, rabeprazole | Irreversibly block H⁺/K⁺-ATPase — the most powerful acid suppressors | Give before breakfast; long use: low magnesium, low vitamin B₁₂, fractures, gut infections |
| Mucosal protectives | Sucralfate, bismuth compounds | Coat the ulcer base | Sucralfate needs acid to act — give on an empty stomach and apart from other drugs; constipation. Bismuth blackens stool and tongue |
| Prostaglandin analogue | Misoprostol | Reduces acid, increases mucus | Prevents NSAID ulcers; diarrhoea; contraindicated in pregnancy (contracts the uterus) |
| Anti-*H. pylori* therapy | PPI + two antibiotics (amoxicillin with clarithromycin or metronidazole), usually for 14 days | Eradicates the bacterium; prevents relapse | Complete the course; metronidazole — no alcohol |

**Uses**: peptic ulcer, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD), Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, prevention of stress ulcers in ICU and of NSAID ulcers, before anaesthesia to reduce aspiration risk.

**Interactions**: antacids reduce absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron and digoxin — give them about 2 hours apart. Omeprazole may reduce the effect of clopidogrel.

**Nursing**: give antacids after meals and at bedtime (or as ordered); shake suspensions; give PPIs before breakfast; teach the patient to avoid smoking, alcohol and NSAIDs, to eat regular meals and to report black stools, vomiting blood or severe pain (signs of bleeding or perforation).

## 2.7 Antidiarrhoeals and fluid–electrolyte therapy

The main danger in diarrhoea is **dehydration and electrolyte loss**, especially in children. Replacing fluid is the most important treatment.

**Oral rehydration solution (ORS)**: a balanced mixture of glucose, sodium chloride, potassium chloride and trisodium citrate. Glucose helps sodium (and therefore water) to be absorbed from the gut by co-transport, which works even during diarrhoea. The WHO/UNICEF **low-osmolarity ORS** reduces stool output and vomiting. In children, **zinc** for 14 days is given along with ORS under the national guidelines (IMNCI).

**IV fluids** in severe dehydration or when the patient cannot drink: Ringer lactate (preferred) or normal saline, with potassium as needed.

**Drugs used in diarrhoea**

| Group | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Antimotility | Loperamide, diphenoxylate with atropine | Slow the gut; not in children, bloody diarrhoea or high fever (can hold the infection in) |
| Antisecretory | Racecadotril | Reduces secretion into the gut |
| Adsorbents | Kaolin, pectin, activated charcoal | Little proven benefit |
| Probiotics | Lactobacillus, *Saccharomyces boulardii* | Restore normal flora; antibiotic-associated diarrhoea |
| Antimicrobials | Metronidazole (amoebiasis, giardiasis), ciprofloxacin or azithromycin (cholera, shigellosis), furazolidone | Only when there is a specific cause; most watery diarrhoea needs no antibiotic |

**Furazolidone**: a nitrofuran antimicrobial acting locally in the gut against many bacteria and *Giardia*; used in bacterial diarrhoea and giardiasis. Side effects: nausea, headache, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (flushing, vomiting) — the patient must avoid alcohol. It also weakly inhibits monoamine oxidase, so foods rich in tyramine and some drugs are avoided.

**Dicyclomine**: an anticholinergic antispasmodic that relaxes smooth muscle of the gut; used for abdominal colic, irritable bowel syndrome and dysmenorrhoea. Side effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast heart rate. Contraindicated in glaucoma, enlarged prostate, intestinal obstruction and in infants under 6 months.

**Nursing in diarrhoea**: assess hydration (thirst, sunken eyes, skin pinch, urine output, weight, pulse, BP); keep an intake–output chart; teach mothers to prepare and give ORS correctly (clean water, whole packet in the stated volume, small frequent sips; continue breastfeeding and feeding); hand hygiene and safe disposal of stools; perianal skin care; observe for danger signs (lethargy, unable to drink, blood in stool).

## Remember

- Antiseptic = living tissue; disinfectant = objects. Clean before you disinfect.
- 70% alcohol works best; glutaraldehyde for endoscopes; hypochlorite for blood spills; soap inactivates chlorhexidine and cetrimide.
- Never induce vomiting in an unconscious patient or after corrosives or kerosene.
- Ondansetron (5-HT₃) for chemotherapy vomiting; hyoscine and antihistamines for motion sickness; metoclopramide can cause dystonia.
- Bulk laxatives need plenty of water; lactulose also treats hepatic encephalopathy; liquid paraffin risks lipid pneumonia.
- PPIs are the strongest acid suppressors — before breakfast; sucralfate on an empty stomach; misoprostol not in pregnancy.
- Mg antacids → diarrhoea, Al antacids → constipation; antacids bind tetracycline, iron, fluoroquinolones.
- ORS is the mainstay in diarrhoea; zinc for children; antimotility drugs not for children or bloody diarrhoea.
- Furazolidone and metronidazole: no alcohol. Dicyclomine: not in glaucoma or infants under 6 months.

# Unit 3: Drugs acting on the respiratory system and the skin

INC Unit IV (2 hours) — antiasthmatics and bronchodilators (salbutamol inhalers), decongestants, expectorants, antitussives and mucolytics, bronchoconstrictors and antihistamines — joined here with INC Unit VII (1 hour) — drugs for the skin: antihistamines and antipruritics, benzyl benzoate, gamma BHC, clotrimazole, miconazole and silver sulfadiazine for burns. The two units are taught together because antihistamines belong to both. Doses are not given; follow the prescriber's order.

## 3.1 Asthma and COPD in brief

In **bronchial asthma**, allergens, infection, cold air, exercise, smoke or drugs (aspirin, β-blockers) trigger an inflammatory response in sensitive airways. Mast cells release histamine and leukotrienes → bronchial smooth muscle contracts, the mucosa swells and thick mucus is produced. The patient has wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough, often worse at night. In **COPD** (chronic bronchitis and emphysema, usually from smoking) the airflow limitation is largely fixed.

Two kinds of drug are needed:

```text
 ASTHMA DRUGS
 ├── Relievers (bronchodilators) — open the airway quickly
 │     β₂ agonists, anticholinergics, methylxanthines
 └── Controllers (preventers) — reduce inflammation over time
       inhaled corticosteroids, leukotriene antagonists,
       mast cell stabilisers, anti-IgE antibody
```

## 3.2 Bronchodilators

**β₂-adrenergic agonists** — stimulate β₂ receptors on bronchial muscle → cAMP rises → relaxation.

| Type | Examples | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short-acting (SABA) | Salbutamol, terbutaline | Quick relief of an attack; before exercise |
| Long-acting (LABA) | Salmeterol, formoterol | Long-term control, only together with an inhaled steroid |

- Routes: inhaler (metered-dose or dry-powder), nebuliser, oral, injection. Inhalation is preferred: rapid action with fewer side effects.
- Side effects: tremor of the hands, palpitations, tachycardia, nervousness, headache, low potassium (with frequent use), muscle cramps.
- Terbutaline and salbutamol relax the uterus too, so they have been used to delay preterm labour.
- Caution in heart disease, hyperthyroidism and diabetes.
- Interactions: non-selective β-blockers (propranolol) block their effect and may provoke bronchospasm.

**Anticholinergics** — ipratropium (short-acting), tiotropium (long-acting). Block muscarinic receptors in the airways → bronchodilation and less mucus. Preferred in COPD; ipratropium added to salbutamol in acute severe asthma. Side effects: dry mouth, bitter taste; caution in glaucoma (keep the nebuliser mist away from the eyes) and enlarged prostate.

**Methylxanthines** — theophylline, aminophylline (IV form), doxofylline. Relax bronchial muscle (phosphodiesterase inhibition and adenosine blockade) and stimulate breathing.
- Narrow therapeutic index; blood levels are monitored.
- Side effects: nausea, vomiting, restlessness, insomnia, tachycardia, arrhythmias and convulsions at high levels.
- Interactions: levels rise with erythromycin, ciprofloxacin and cimetidine (enzyme inhibitors) and fall in smokers and with rifampicin.
- Aminophylline is given by slow IV injection or infusion only.

## 3.3 Anti-inflammatory (controller) drugs

**Corticosteroids** — the most effective controllers.
- Inhaled: beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone. Reduce airway inflammation, mucus and hyper-reactivity; regular daily use prevents attacks; they do not relieve an acute attack.
- Side effects of inhaled steroids: oral thrush (candidiasis) and hoarseness — **rinse mouth and gargle after each use**; a spacer reduces deposition in the mouth.
- Systemic: oral prednisolone, IV hydrocortisone in acute severe asthma (side effects in Unit 6).

**Leukotriene receptor antagonist** — montelukast: blocks leukotriene action; oral; used for mild asthma, exercise-induced asthma and allergic rhinitis. Report mood changes or sleep disturbance.

**Mast cell stabilisers** — sodium cromoglycate, ketotifen: prevent release of histamine from mast cells. Prophylaxis only; useless in an acute attack.

**Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody** — omalizumab (SC injection) for severe allergic asthma.

## 3.4 Acute severe asthma — what the nurse does

1. Sit the patient upright; stay calm and reassure.
2. Give oxygen as ordered and monitor SpO₂.
3. Give nebulised salbutamol (with ipratropium if ordered); systemic steroid as ordered.
4. Monitor respiratory rate, pulse, speech (can the patient finish a sentence?), use of accessory muscles, peak flow and SpO₂.
5. Danger signs to report at once: silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, falling pulse rate.
6. Avoid sedatives — they depress breathing.

## 3.5 Inhaler technique — teaching the patient

**Metered-dose inhaler (MDI)**

1. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler.
2. Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
3. Seal the lips around the mouthpiece (or use a spacer).
4. Start a slow deep breath and press the canister once at the same time.
5. Continue breathing in slowly and deeply.
6. Hold the breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
7. Wait about a minute before a second puff if ordered.
8. After a steroid inhaler, rinse the mouth and spit.

A **spacer** with a mask is used for children and anyone who cannot coordinate pressing and breathing. **Dry-powder inhalers** need a fast, deep breath and must not be shaken or breathed into. A **nebuliser** turns a solution into a mist through a mask — useful in severe attacks and small children. Teach the patient to carry the reliever at all times, to know the triggers, and to check the dose counter.

## 3.6 Decongestants

Nasal decongestants are α-adrenergic agonists that constrict the swollen blood vessels of the nasal mucosa.

- Topical: xylometazoline, oxymetazoline, phenylephrine nasal drops/sprays. Quick relief in colds and sinusitis, and before nasal procedures. Using them for more than a few days causes **rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa)**.
- Oral: pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine — often in "cold" combinations. They can raise blood pressure and heart rate, cause insomnia and urinary retention.
- Avoid or use with care in hypertension, heart disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, enlarged prostate, and with MAO inhibitors. Saline drops are safest for infants.

## 3.7 Expectorants, mucolytics and antitussives

Cough is a protective reflex. A **productive** (wet) cough should not be suppressed; a **dry, irritating** cough that disturbs sleep may be suppressed.

| Group | Examples | How they act | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expectorants | Guaifenesin, ammonium chloride, potassium iodide; steam inhalation | Increase the volume and looseness of respiratory secretions so they are coughed out | Plenty of oral fluids helps most |
| Mucolytics | Bromhexine, ambroxol, carbocisteine, acetylcysteine | Break mucus fibres and lower viscosity | Acetylcysteine nebulisation can cause bronchospasm (give with a bronchodilator) |
| Antitussives – opioid | Codeine, pholcodine | Depress the cough centre | Drowsiness, constipation, dependence; not for children under 12 years |
| Antitussives – non-opioid | Dextromethorphan, noscapine | Depress the cough centre | Little sedation; no analgesia |
| Antihistamines | Diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine | Sedation and drying of secretions | In many cough syrups |
| Demulcents | Lozenges, honey, glycerin syrups | Soothe the throat | Safe |

**Nursing**: assess the cough (dry or productive, sputum colour, amount, blood); encourage fluids, steam inhalation, deep breathing and chest physiotherapy; do not give suppressants in productive cough or COPD with thick sputum; warn about drowsiness with codeine and antihistamine syrups; keep syrups away from children.

## 3.8 Bronchoconstrictors

Drugs that narrow the airways are mainly important because they can **worsen asthma**:

- **Histamine** and **methacholine** — used only in a controlled bronchial challenge test to diagnose airway hyper-reactivity.
- **Non-selective β-blockers** (propranolol) and even β₁-selective ones at high levels — contraindicated in asthma.
- **Cholinergic drugs** (neostigmine, pilocarpine) — increase bronchial secretions and constriction.
- **Aspirin and other NSAIDs** — in aspirin-sensitive asthma.
- Adenosine, some contrast media.

Always ask a patient with asthma about these drugs and check orders before giving them.

## 3.9 Antihistamines (H₁-receptor antagonists)

Histamine is stored in mast cells and basophils. Through **H₁ receptors** it causes bronchoconstriction, vasodilatation, increased capillary permeability (swelling, wheals), itching and sneezing; through **H₂ receptors** it increases gastric acid.

| Generation | Examples | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, cyproheptadine, dimenhydrinate | Enter the brain → drowsiness; anticholinergic effects; antiemetic and anti-motion-sickness effects |
| Second | Cetirizine, levocetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine | Little or no sedation; once-daily |

**Uses**: allergic rhinitis, urticaria and itching, allergic conjunctivitis, insect bites, drug reactions, motion sickness and vomiting (first generation), sleep (promethazine), and as an add-on in anaphylaxis — **adrenaline is the first drug in anaphylaxis, not an antihistamine**.

**Side effects**: sedation, poor concentration, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention; paradoxical excitement in children; confusion and falls in the elderly.

**Contraindications/cautions**: glaucoma, enlarged prostate, driving or operating machines, with alcohol or other sedatives, very young infants.

**Nursing**: give sedating antihistamines at bedtime; warn not to drive; keep the bed rails up for elderly patients; mouth care for dryness; ask about other sedatives and alcohol.

## 3.10 Antipruritics

Itching (pruritus) is treated by removing the cause and by:
- **Oral antihistamines** (hydroxyzine, cetirizine, chlorpheniramine).
- **Calamine lotion** (zinc oxide and ferric oxide): soothing and cooling; shake before use.
- **Menthol and camphor** in creams: cooling.
- **Crotamiton**: antipruritic that also acts against scabies mites.
- **Topical corticosteroids** for inflammatory itchy rashes (eczema): apply a thin layer, not on broken or infected skin, avoid long use on the face (thinning of skin).
- Emollients for dry skin.

Nursing: keep nails short, cool cotton clothes, avoid hot baths and strong soaps, pat skin dry.

## 3.11 Drugs for scabies and lice

**Scabies** is caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei*; it spreads by close contact.

**Benzyl benzoate**
- Acts by killing mites and their eggs; applied as an emulsion.
- Method: after a bath, dry the skin and apply over the whole body from the neck down (in infants including scalp and face, avoiding eyes), especially between fingers, wrists, axillae, genitals and under nails; leave on and repeat as prescribed.
- Side effects: burning and irritation (worse on broken skin), contact dermatitis; avoid the eyes and mucous membranes. It is diluted for children as directed.

**Gamma benzene hexachloride (gamma BHC, lindane)**
- An organochlorine that kills mites and lice by acting on their nervous system.
- It can be absorbed through skin and cause nerve toxicity, including convulsions, especially in infants, young children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, the elderly and people with broken skin or seizures. For this reason it is restricted or withdrawn in many countries and is not the first choice now.
- Applied only once to cool, dry skin (not after a hot bath, which increases absorption), and washed off after the prescribed time.

**Preferred now**: permethrin cream (topical, first choice) or oral ivermectin. Crotamiton is an alternative.

**Nursing for scabies**: treat all close contacts at the same time; wash clothes, towels and bed linen in hot water and dry in the sun; items that cannot be washed are sealed in a bag for a few days; trim nails; explain that itching may continue for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment and does not mean failure.

## 3.12 Topical antifungals: clotrimazole and miconazole

Both are **imidazole** antifungals. They inhibit the fungal enzyme that makes ergosterol (an essential part of the fungal cell membrane) → the membrane leaks and the fungus dies.

- **Uses**: ringworm (tinea corporis, cruris, pedis), cutaneous and vaginal candidiasis, oral thrush (clotrimazole lozenges, miconazole oral gel), pityriasis versicolor, fungal ear infections.
- **Forms**: cream, powder, lotion, vaginal pessary or cream, oral gel or troche.
- **Side effects**: local burning, itching, redness; rarely contact allergy.
- **Interaction**: miconazole oral gel is absorbed enough to increase the effect of warfarin (bleeding) — report bruising.
- **Nursing/teaching**: clean and dry the area; apply a thin layer beyond the edge of the lesion; continue for 2 weeks after the skin looks clear to prevent relapse; keep skin folds dry; use separate towels; vaginal preparations at bedtime, and treat the partner if advised.

## 3.13 Silver sulfadiazine in burns

- Combines silver (toxic to bacteria) with a sulfonamide; broad spectrum, including *Pseudomonas* and *Staphylococcus*, and some *Candida*.
- **Use**: prevention and treatment of infection in second- and third-degree burns; also some leg ulcers.
- Applied as a cream with a sterile gloved hand or spatula to the cleaned burn, covered or left exposed as per unit policy; old cream is gently removed at each dressing change.
- **Side effects**: burning or itching, skin discoloration, transient fall in white cell count, allergy in people sensitive to sulfonamides.
- **Avoid**: sulfonamide allergy, late pregnancy and newborns in the first months of life (risk of kernicterus), G6PD deficiency (caution).
- **Nursing**: strict asepsis; give analgesia before dressing; observe the wound for infection (smell, colour of discharge, fever); monitor white cell count when large areas are treated; maintain fluids and nutrition.

## 3.14 General rules for applying topical drugs

1. Check the order, the site and the patient; wear gloves.
2. Clean and dry the skin; remove old applications gently.
3. Apply thinly in the direction of hair growth; do not rub too hard.
4. Do not apply on broken skin unless the drug is meant for wounds.
5. Watch for local irritation and allergy; record and report.

## Remember

- Salbutamol (SABA) = reliever; inhaled steroid = controller; LABA always with a steroid.
- β₂ agonists: tremor, tachycardia, low potassium. Theophylline: narrow index; levels rise with erythromycin and ciprofloxacin.
- Rinse the mouth after inhaled steroids (thrush, hoarseness).
- MDI: shake, breathe out, press and breathe in slowly, hold about 10 seconds.
- Nasal decongestants for a few days only (rebound congestion).
- Do not suppress a productive cough; codeine not in children under 12.
- Non-selective β-blockers and aspirin can provoke bronchospasm in asthma.
- First-generation antihistamines sedate; adrenaline, not an antihistamine, is first in anaphylaxis.
- Scabies: treat all contacts; permethrin is first choice now; lindane (gamma BHC) is neurotoxic.
- Clotrimazole and miconazole block ergosterol synthesis; continue 2 weeks after clearing.
- Silver sulfadiazine for burns; avoid in sulfa allergy, late pregnancy and newborns.
